utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted and Thomas Laugel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Mr. Hadzic, good morning Counsel. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I take it you will testify in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please give us your name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Jakub Bijak. I was born on the 5th of November, 1977.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Bijak, you are about to make the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I must point out to you that by doing so you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give untruthful information to this Tribunal. May I ask you to give the solemn declaration -- to make the solemn declaration now that the Court Usher will hand over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Bijak.

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I have to remind myself as well as you that since we're both speaking English, we have to be quite careful not to overlap and give the translators an opportunity to translate what we say into B/C/S. I want to begin today by talking about your professional and educational background. First of all, where are you currently employed?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: I am currently a lecturer at the University of Southampton in the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how long have you held that position for?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Since February 2009.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what is the subject matter of your work?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: I work in the area of demography and social statistics. So basically I deal professionally with population change and consequences and causes thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now prior to that position, where did you work?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: I started my professional career back in 1999 as a three-month research fellow at the Netherlands Institute for Demographic Research. After which I continued my masters studies back in Poland. And after that, I had two yearly positions at the United Nations International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia in the demographic unit, for a year as a research assistant and then for another year as a demographer. Since then I have worked between 2003 and -- early 2009 in Central European Forum for Migration and Population Research in Warsaw, which was a joint venture between the International Organisation for Migration, a Swiss foundation for population migration and the environment, and other organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's first talk about your position at the Central European Forum. What was your focus there?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: The focus was the research on migration, especially in the context of population change.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And while you were at the Office of the Prosecution for the ICTY, what was the subject matter of your work?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: The subject matter was the reconstruction of demographic consequences of population crisis first of all in Bosnia, this was my first year of the work here, and then also in Croatia in the second year.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I understand you have a masters in quantitative methods and information systems and a doctorate in economics. Can you tell us how are these degrees relevant to the field of demography?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Both my masters and doctorate are strongly linked with demography. In fact, both my masters dissertation as -- and my PhD thesis were related to the field. In particular, the masters dissertation concerned mortality in developed countries, and my doctoral dissertation concerned forecasting migration in Europe under uncertainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 2793. This is tab 16 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Doctor, can you confirm that this is your resume?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: This is my resume current as of early 2012.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Does this page highlight a number of your publications?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes. This page shows several selected publications that are most relevant to the current testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you give us a rough estimate of the number of research reports and other publications that you have authored in the field of demographics?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: I have authored one book monograph and then authored and coauthored over 30 articles and book chapters as well as also over 30 reports, working papers, and other contributions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit P2012. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Doctor, have you testified as an expert witness before?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 2831 on the screen. This is tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We have before us an expert report entitled: "Pre-war ethnic composition of, and population displacements from war-affected areas of Croatia in the period 25 June 1991 - 31 December 1993," dated June 2012. Is this your expert report?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes. This is the expert report I coauthored with my colleagues Amie Kamanda and Sarah Lubman.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you've just mentioned that you coauthored it. Can you tell us, these two other contributors, who they were and what was their contribution?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Both Amie and Sarah are my doctoral students who for this report acted as research assistants and contributed two sections of the report. Amie Kamanda contributed section 3 and Sarah Lubman contributed section 5. Further to that, they provided comments to the overall report, but that notwithstanding, I remain the main author of the report and I take the whole responsibility for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So I take it you directly supervised their work?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Generally what were -- what are the objectives or what were the main objectives of this report?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: This report as stated in the executive summary and then in the introduction had two main objectives. The first one was to examine the ethnic composition in the war-affected areas of Croatia based on the data from the 1991 population census. The second objective was to examine population displacements from the war-affected areas between 25th of June, 1991, and the end of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What territory falls within the scope of your report?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: In this report we have followed the official Croatian government definition of war-affected areas as defined in the Croatian law which is cited in the report. And for the purpose of this particular case, we excluded the territories around Dubrovnik as clearly not relevant. So basically we analysed population composition and displacements from the areas of -- which can be labeled as Krajina, Western Slavonia, as well as Eastern Slavonia Baranja and Western Sirmium or Srem or Srijem, which we, the latter, refer to collectively as Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you tell us a little bit more about these war-affected areas that were determined under Croatian law? Does this mean that with regard to some municipalities in Croatia, you only considered certain parts of those municipalities? You didn't consider the complete municipality?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes, this is true. The area in the studies shown in -- on -- in figure 1 on the sixth page of the report where the red dots indicate settlements, so localities, that are considered to be war affected according to the Croatian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to that page. I think it's page 7 in the e-court. Page 6 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you tell us how well did the -- or do the war-affected areas correspond to the three Serbian autonomous districts that were created in 1991 and that eventually became the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: From the information that we received from the Office of the Prosecutor, it seems that these areas quite well correspond to the areas of the Serb autonomous regions as they were declared but not necessarily as they ended up being actually controlled by the Croatian Serbs in -- as of early 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And perhaps explain to us. We see that -- within the blue boundaries, we see certain white areas. What would those constitute?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: The white areas within blue boundaries are those parts of the areas that were declared as Serb autonomous areas that were actually never involved in any way in -- directly in the conflict and, hence, haven't been labeled as areas of special state care, which is the shortcut for war-affected areas in the Croatian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I just notice looking at this figure that in the Western Krajina area on the eastern side there are a number of war-affected areas that are even outside the boundaries of the SAO Western Krajina -- or -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yeah, this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Western Slavonia, I'm sorry. I correct myself.

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: In Western Slavonia there is a group of municipalities -- there is a group of settlements in the municipalities that were as of 1992 outside of the Serb control yet still are considered to be war-affected by Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you know just off the top of your head, would those be settlements that perhaps were under Croatian government control that they took back during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mention in your report that, in 1991, there were 102 municipalities in Croatia while, in 1997, this number had increased to 538. Can you tell us what impact, if any, did this change in the number of municipalities have on your analysis?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: The new municipal division that was introduced since 1992 enabled a more fine-grained look into the ethnic composition and the displacements of persons from the war-affected areas because the pre-war municipalities were quite large, and as such, the patterns that we could observe for the pre-war municipalities could be actually masked by the sides. Whereas for the post-war municipalities, the patterns could be seen much clearly. That is why in the report we present -- well, we present both, old municipalities and new municipalities, if not in the main text then in the appendices.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, looking at the municipalities as they existed in 1997 simply allowed you to look at the data in more detail. It didn't actually change your figures?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: No, they did not change the figures at all. They are just a different way of aggregating them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have figure 5 of your report on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is page 16 of the report. It would be page 17 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And while that's coming up on the screen, Doctor, could you explain to us why was 25 June 1991 selected as the initial date for your study?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: This was a part of the terms of reference I have received for this report from the Office of the Prosecutor, but also just to corroborate on that, what we did is we looked at the patterns of population displacements from the database -- from the main database that we were using - I will talk about this in a moment - and we have seen that there was a visible change in the patterns on or about the 25th of June, 1991. Whereas before that date, the daily average of displacements from the war-affected areas was about 60 persons per day. Since 25th of June, in the last six days of the month, this number has increased to close to 500 persons per day. So clearly something important has happened on or about the 25th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Looking at this figure 5, we see that there is a peak at the beginning of June and there is also a peak on the 15th of June. Can you tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: These peaks are quite likely statistical artefacts, so they might indicate that some of the dates were missing or had the date element missing in which case they would be most often recorded as if something happened on the first day of the month. The peaks on the 20th, 15th, and also 10th of June indicate something that is known in statistics as heaping, which is the -- a form of a recall bias, which means that sometimes due to problems with recollection of events, the dates are being rounded to the nearest five or ten, and this seems to show in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So just by way of an example, if I was a displaced person and I was being interviewed in 1994, I might say, "Well, I was displaced in June sometime around the beginning," and that would most likely be recorded as the 1st of June?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes. That's perfectly plausible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now for purposes of this report, did you look at the causes of displacement?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: We did not since this information was not available to us in the sources that we have examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I think at this stage it would be useful if you could just give us a brief overview of the structure of your report.

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: The report as stated in the introduction is structured into six main sections and a number of appendices. So after a brief executive summary, the report starts with an introduction which introduces the aims, scope, terminology of the report, and also defines the area under study. Then section 2 addresses the first aim of the report, which is the analyses of the ethnic composition of the war-affected areas. Sections 3, 4, and 5 address the second aim of the report, which is the analyses of displacements. And in particular, section 3 looks at the available scientific literature on the topic; section 4 analyses the database from the government office -- government office of displaced persons and refugees; and section 5 looks at other possible sources of data that we could -- that we could obtain as being publicly available. Then section 6 includes the main conclusions of the study, followed by a list of references and links to the ICTY material, followed by five appendices. The first one dealing with the territorial divisions of the area under study; the second one, appendix B, to the profiles of the municipalities that were included in the study; appendix C, to selected settlements within war-affected areas; appendix D presents some summary maps in the new municipal division to supplement the old municipal division which is shown in the report; and finally, appendix E provides brief biographical notes of all the three authors.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just turning quickly to appendix C, can you tell us how did you go about selecting the settlements for that appendix?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: For that appendix, three of the settlements, so Vukovar, Ilok, and Erdut, were selected on the basis of them being mentioned in the indictment. The further settlements that are listed in the appendix were those for which we found that there was a substantial number of displacements during the period under study. And by that, we mean that we set a threshold of 2.000 displaced persons, so we are showing all the settlements where the number of displaced persons exceeded the threshold.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would like to now talk about the statistical sources that you used in conducting your analysis. But before we do that, could you tell us, what do demographers typically use to arrive at figures regarding population shifts?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Normally demographers would look at sources of information such as population censuses such as the registration of population, the registration of vital events, the registration of migratory events, registration of other events of interest, as well as different surveys, if relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what about scientific -- scientific and academic sources or secondary sources, as you may call them, are they typically used?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes, this is -- this is basically the main part of every piece of academic work, to review the literature that is already available on the topic. Not only to check what has already been done but also to provide a bench-mark for one's own study.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what types of sources were available to you in your analysis for this report?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: For the first aim of this report, we had available aggregate tables from the 1991 population census carried out in the Republic of Croatia. For the second aim of the report, we identified a number of published sources which are listed in the references section of the report. And most importantly, we were able to look at the data provided to the Office of the Prosecutor by the Croatian authorities following your request back in 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And did you also look at international reports; for instance, by UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes, we did. These international reports constitute a vast part of section 5 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you tell us when was the next -- next census conducted in Croatia after 1991?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: The next census was conducted in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And why did you not use that census for purposes of your analysis?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: There were several reasons for that. Firstly, the date of the first post-war census was too far away from the period under study to provide any useful information for our report. Secondly, between the end of the period under study and the next census, 2001, there were significant population shifts within Croatia in 1995, after the operations Flash and Storm, which would have distorted any inferences that we could have made on the basis of the post-war census.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to talk about each of the sources that you've mentioned. First, when was the population census for Croatia taken? Or in other words, when was it -- when was it completed, let's say?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: The census date was the 31st of March, 1911, so that was the reference date. But of course the actual data collection took place a bit later when the people who were enumerated in the census were asked to recall the circumstances on the day of the 31st of March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. And I was about to correct you. I think you said something about close to 1911. But this is 1991.

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: This is 1991, apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that the census was completed before the conflict began in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: For the benefit of the interpreters, could you please pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, I didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No problem. Would it be correct to say that the census would have been completed before the conflict began in Croatia in full scale?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now who conducted the census?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: It was the Croatian Office for Statistics or, back then, the Yugoslav Croatian Republican Office for Statistics that conducted the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who was included in the census?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: In principle the census should have included the whole permanent population, permanently resident population of Croatia. So these were the people with the legal status of the permanent residents of the territory of Croatia at the time of the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you give us an idea of how the census was conducted? Maybe explain the process in general terms.

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: The process consisted in enumerators going from a household to a household and interviewing persons in that household as to the basic socio-demographic characteristics and filling census forms, which were later computerized in the statistical office in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us what kind of information was collected --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's probably because I am not waiting for you to complete your answer. But let me repeat my question: What information was essentially collected from each person? What kind of data?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: The main demographic characteristics, such as a person's sex, date of birth, marital status, number of children born for women. Additionally, some socio-economic characteristics about the person and about the households, as well as for those households that were linked to agricultural production, some information about the farms.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And was this type of information and this process typical of house censuses that are conducted around the world?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes. This was typical, especially back in 1991. Of course, since then, the computerization has progressed so that there are technological advances in census-taking, but this was, you know, a perfectly standard procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what was the process for reporting ethnicity to the census?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Ethnicity in the census was a self-recorded category, so basically a person could have reported themselves as being a Croat, a Serb, a Hungarian, a Yugoslav, or they could equally well decline to declare themselves ethnically.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if they declined declaring ethnicity, what happened?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Nothing. They would just be recorded as those who didn't declare their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now you mentioned that the questionnaires were computerized or inserted into a computer system. Can you tell us, was any quality control imposed by the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I haven't objected up until now, but I think we should lay some foundation for the witness's knowledge of this particular information.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, before I proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what are you basing your knowledge on the Croatian census?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: There is -- part of it is the literature cited in the report, including the 1991 census report, and part of this information comes from the work I conducted on the census for Bosnia-Herzegovina, also whilst at the Tribunal. Back at the time, back in 1991 the -- both the Bosnian and the Croatian censuses followed the standard Yugoslav rules for census taking.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And while you were working for the Office of the Prosecution, did you take any trips down to Croatia and speak with officials who were responsible for the census back in 1991 and forward in time?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We undertook such a mission, if I remember correctly, in July 2003 or thereabouts, and we spent a week and a half at the premises of the statistical office in Zagreb, and we talked to the people responsible for data collection at the statistical office. And also we were able to do some analysis of the material on location.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And based on the information that you had that you described for us, could you tell us what kind of quality control the Croatian authorities imposed upon the data they were collecting for the census?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: I do not know exactly what checks were conducted in the case of Croatian data, but the standard routine procedures would be logical consistency checks; so making sure, for example, that the person's date of birth as reported is earlier than the census date, for example. Or that the first name matches with the reported gender. Then the other type of consistency checks that are usually carried out are related to the duplicate control, whereby the statistical authorities check that a person is mentioned in the census only once, because it happens that during the enumeration process some people are being reported twice. A well-known example considers children of divorced parents who are quite often reported both by the father as well as by the mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have 65 ter 851 on the screen. Just for cross-referencing purposes, this is the same document that is P1776. But for reasons that will become obvious, I am showing the witness this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: First, can you confirm, is this the 1991 population census in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And perhaps we can turn randomly into the document. Maybe let's go to page 150.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The first 200 pages of this census primarily contain various charts. Could you tell us what's contained in these charts?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: This particular publication deals with the ethnic breakdown of the population of the Republic of Croatia, and different tables within this publication show the number of people who declare themselves according to specific ethnic affiliations. So this -- this -- what is on the screen shows an excerpt of such a table for some selected municipalities and settlements.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn now to page 275.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: After these charts there are a series of maps, and I want to show you the one for Osijek municipality. Doctor, can you tell us what is represented by the various coloured circles on this map?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: The circles represent particular settlements within -- within the Osijek municipality. The colours denote the type of ethnic majority in a given settlement, and the size of the circle corresponds to the number of people living in a given place. So for example, the town of Osijek clearly stands out as the largest settlement in this municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now what about the circles that have an empty centre, what do those represent?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: The filled versus empty circles represent different types of ethnic majority. So the solid circles represent the absolute majority, so where a dominant group considered 50 per cent or more of the total population. And in this case, the red colour denotes Croats and the blue colour denotes Serbs. Whereas the empty -- the circles with the empty interior denote settlements with relative majority, so those who were the dominant ethnic group had a majority yet still below 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we see above the map there is a number of figures. Are those from the results of the census?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes, they are. All the information in this publication is supposed to come from the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we mentioned this in an e-mail last week. We would like to substitute this original version of the census with the one that's under P1776 simply because this one has the coloured maps and, as you can see, the colour is relevant to understanding these maps. I can do that by written motion or, if you would like, we could probably just do it orally?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And is P1776 in B/C/S as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It's an identical document except for 1776 is all black and white.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we don't -- we didn't interpret the whole -- we didn't translate the entire census because you have a template and, from that, I think you can basically understand the rest of the document since it's in the Latin script.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Any objection from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: As long as the Prosecution proffers that they are the same documents except for the colour, there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So we will substitute this document. Mr. Registrar, will this document then have the exhibit number P1 -- whatever it is, 1776, or will it have a new number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, correct, Your Honours. 65 ter document 851 shall replace and become the Prosecution Exhibit P1776. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Doctor, I now want to talk about the 1994 database that was created by the Croatian government Office for Displaced Persons, Returnees, and Refugees, which I think we can refer to as ODPRR. Can you tell us what was this 1994 database?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: The 1994 database includes a collection of information from -- about the displaced persons in the territories of Croatia to which the Croatian government had access at the time. And this was the first comprehensive data collection under -- undertaken by the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees. Before that, of course data on refugees were collected, but the 1994 database is the first time when actually all the -- all the displaced persons had to register themselves and confirm their status in -- to Croatian authorities, which information was later -- and later entered into a database. So for the first time, the whole comprehensive information about displaced persons was -- became available in electronic format.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you tell us, how do you define displaced persons for purposes of your report?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: In our report as stated on -- on page 4, we define displaced persons as those officially recognised as such due to war-related activities by appropriate national or international authorities. And this is a term -- this is a generic term. We referred to displaced persons in the context of both internally displaced persons as well as refugees, so those who moved abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to go back to your answer before this last one. You mentioned that the 1994 database covers those displaced persons to which the government had access. Can you clarify that for us. Does that mean that in areas that were not under the Croatian government control, those displaced persons would not be part of the database?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. The database only relates to the displaced persons who were at the time in the government-controlled territories of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And does the database include refugees in third countries, either Serbia or Bosnia, but as well as places like Germany, Hungary, and other parts of Europe and the world?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: No, it does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you tell us, based upon what you know about this 1994 database, was it mandatory for all displaced persons in Croatian government-controlled area to register themselves with the ODPRR?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: No, it was not mandatory. A person could register, especially if they wanted to receive some state assistance stemming from the fact that they were a displaced person. But, of course if someone was displaced, there was always an option of not disclosing themselves to the authorities; for example, if people lived with their families and didn't need state support, they could equally be not be registered as displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And to be included in the 1994 ODPRR database, did the person have to still have been a displaced person in a Croat government-controlled area in 1994?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, the person should have been either a displaced persons -- either a displaced person or a returnee by the time of the -- of the 1994 registration; although, the returns and returnees data were not fully collected until the later re-registration that took place in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we will talk about the 1997 database in a minute. But if I understand you correctly, if a person prior to 1994, a displaced person, decided to change his permanent residence to the place to which he was displaced to, he would not appear in the 1994 database?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: The person would still appear in the 1994 database if they were a displaced person, so a person with entitlement to be called as such. And the report mentions the situations this was a person could have ceased to be a displaced persons. This is listed -- the circumstances are listed in footnote 14 on the page 15 of the report. So in this -- in this case, a displaced person would cease to be such if the municipality of the person's former place of residence decided that the person can actually return safely to their place of residence. The person decided out of their own free will to return or the person did not accept assistance from the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And in such cases, those persons would not appear in the 1994 database?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: I think -- I think this is the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you tell us, when did the collection of the data for the 1994 database begin?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: The original collection took place in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if you know, could you tell us in what form was the data collected?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: So the data was primarily collected first using paper forms which were then computerized and stored centrally in a database of the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And was this 1994 database limited to one ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: In principle it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you tell us, how was the date and place of displacement determined?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: In the 1994 collection, the date and place of displacement are as reported by the person in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you tell us based upon your meetings with Croatian officials while you were with the Office of the Prosecution, were you informed of what measures the Croatian authorities employed to ensure the accuracy of the data in the 1994 database?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes. They have conducted a range of quality checks, most importantly consisting of duplicate removal from the 1994 and later collections.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what incentive did the Croatian authorities have to ensure the accuracy of the data contained within this database?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: I think that the main incentives they had was the fact that the registration of a person as a displaced person bear financial consequences for the Croatian government, so basically people registered as displaced persons were entitled to a range of benefits, which is why it was in the interest of the government, and hence the office, to get the numbers as correct as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When did the OTP obtain this database?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, it was in May 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what measures were taken to, let's say, clean the data?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: We -- first of all, we double-checked the data collections we received from the point of view of presence of the duplicates, and we managed to identify several more of those and removed them from the database.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were individual entries within the ODPRR database matched with the 1991 census?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Partially. We have matched some of the collections including the one, which I will talk about a bit later, that concerns the registration of displaced persons in Eastern Slavonia in 1997 and the requests for return, but we didn't match the 1994 and 1997 collections.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us why you did not match the 1994 database?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: This was mainly for the -- because of the time constraint we had whilst on the mission to Zagreb. All the -- the whole matching process had to be carried out whilst in Zagreb under controlled conditions to ensure the privacy, protection, and at the time we were able only to -- to match a limited number of collections, and we prioritised the 1997 registration in Eastern Slavonia and requests for return because there was an acute need to supplement this information with data on ethnicity, as will become obvious later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your report also mentions a 1997 re-registration database that was created by ODPRR. Could you tell us what that database was and how you used it in your analysis?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: This was an endeavour by -- the Croatian authorities undertook in 1997 to verify the numbers of displaced persons, of returnees, of refugees in Croatia, done with -- with -- presumably with the aim of establishing a sound evidence base for the payments of the associated benefits.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now why did you not rely on the 1997 database?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: There were two partially overlapping reasons for that. One was that the 1997 database relates to a year which is further away from the end of the period under study. So this is -- this is already almost four years after the end of the period under study. And secondly, the size of the collection is smaller than the 1994 one because between 1994 and 1997, quite a lot of people have already lost their entitlement to state support and hence were not included in the 1997 re-registration.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was there a significant overlap between the 1994 and 1997 databases nonetheless?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes, there was. And actually, the collections were already cross-matched by the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees in Zagreb, and they identified about 80 per cent of the 1997 registered displaced persons back in the 1994 database.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What were the advantages -- or what are the advantages of the 1994 database from a demographic perspective?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Well, first of all, in the context of this report, the 1994 database relates to a period just after the end of the period under study in this report. Secondly, the way in which some items are being reported is also better from the analytical point of view. For example, the date of displacement in the 1994 collection is as reported by the person themselves, whereas in the 1997 collection, the only date available is the date of the first acquisition of a status of a displaced person, which might be, well, a bit later than the actual displacement took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And now could you tell us what are the drawbacks of the 1994 database from a demographical point of view?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: The main drawback, of course, is that this data set does not cover the whole area of Croatia. It only covers those areas which were at the time under the government -- Croatian government control. It also does not include refugees from Croatia. So basically there are some important population of displaced persons and refugees who are not included in this particular data set.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now what about data regarding displaced Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: There are some data about the displaced Serbs in the 1994 collection but they are really few and far between. The main information about the displaced Serbs that I use in the report comes from the 1997 registration of displaced persons in Eastern Slavonia and the related requests for return filed with the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we'll turn to that database in just one minute, but quickly, was there an effort when you were working for the Office of the Prosecution to obtain data regarding Serb displacement from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes, they were -- there were such attempts and we have filed several requests for assistance to the Serb -- Serbian authorities at the time but they were actually never answered during my time at the ICTY nor to my knowledge after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Turning to the last database, the one that you just mentioned, what is the 1997 request for return and Eastern Slavonian registration database? Who was including them there?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: So in 1997, in the territories of Eastern Slavonia, before that territory was reintegrated into the Croatian administrative system, under the auspices of the United Nations there was a registration of displaced persons carried out in the region, and also in parallel, people from anywhere, and this includes non-government-controlled areas of Croatia, this includes -- in Eastern Slavonia, this includes Serbia and Montenegro, and Bosnia-Herzegovina and other places, could have lodged requests for return to Croatian authorities if they wished to return to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you tell us to what extent did the data in this database overlap with the data from the 1994 and 1997 ODPRR databases?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Theoretically there should be no or hardly any overlap because of the very different subpopulations that were subject to these different registrations processes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You said "theoretically." How did it turn out? We'll go more into the actual data you found from this 1997 database, but just generally, was there -- did you find significant overlap?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Actually, we did not check for overlap between these collections because the 1997 re-registration and the request for return were still left waiting for any data that might have come from Serbia as -- at the time that I was working at the OTP. So this part of the work remained unfinished.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You also mention -- you've also mentioned that one of your sources were international reports such as UNHCR reports. To what extent did you rely on such reports for your analysis?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: We basically used these reports as a way of corroborating our findings and just benchmarking our findings against something that was provided by mostly international authorities that could be seen as impartial and nonpartisan.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And with regard to the remaining secondary sources that are cited in your report, government reports, scientific or academic literature, to what extent did you rely on those sources in arriving at your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: To a similar extent, mainly to provide the background information and also to cross-check our results against those cited with the proviso that in quite a few cases, especially when it comes to academic literature, it was obvious that the authors had their own agenda when they published their results. So we did not treat these sources at the same level as we would, for example, treat the UNHCR estimates.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did these sources, nonetheless, have some value for the purposes of your report?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes, they do. Especially from the point of view of confirming and corroborating the findings that we have reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. I now want to turn to the conclusions in your report. Based on your analysis of the 1994 ODPRR database, you determined that 182.995 persons were displaced between 25 June 1991 and 31 December 1993 from the war-affected areas in Croatia and that over 97 per cent of them were Croats and other non-Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you also indicate in your report that this 182.955 figure is a minimum confirmed estimate. Why is that?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: This is mainly for the reasons that I already mentioned, that the data collection took place only in the government-controlled areas of Croatia. So the -- there must have been displaced persons outside of the government-controlled areas of Croatia and there must have been refugees in other countries, and also there were some people who did not register as displaced persons, which all together suggests that the true numbers are higher than the ones we quote in the report. But, of course, we do not know by how much. This is why in the report we presume the numbers, that we are pretty certain that they refer to the -- to the actual -- the minimum conservative estimates of the number of displaced persons. So we -- in the report we wanted to err on the side of caution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Is a third factor that impacts this analysis, as we discussed, the situation where a person has relinquished their displaced persons benefits by 1994 and therefore they would also not be counted?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes. This is -- this is yet another possibility, which is actually something that is confirmed or suggested by the -- by the literature, that they were -- there were some short-term displacements, especially in 1991, which then did not end up in the 1994 database.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Very well. You've just mentioned three --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly make a pause after the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are kindly asking you to make a pause after the end of the answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I just wanted to comment that you've now mentioned three provisos and you've mentioned them in the past, and in the future, we'll just refer to those as the three provisos with regard to the minimum estimate. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now compared to the pre-war population size, in which of the three Serbian autonomous districts in Croatia was the proportion of displaced persons the highest?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we can perhaps turn to page 19 of the report, 20 on e-court. This is 65 ter 2831.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was definitely the case for the broadly defined Eastern Slavonia, so the war-affected areas in the municipalities of Beli Manastir, Osijek, Vukovar, and Vinkovci, where the number of DPs in the 1994 collection amounted to 38.2 per cent of the pre-war population, and on the top of that, from the request for return and the 1997 registration in Eastern Slavonia to further 1.6 per cent. So in terms of the relation between the number of displaced persons and the pre-war population, the Eastern Slavonia region was clearly the highest.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to table 3, which is on page 16 of your report, page 17 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You indicate that the ODPRR database shows 76.226 persons displaced from the SBWS or Eastern Slavonia war-affected areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Scroll down a bit on the page, I think. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Doctor, based on your analysis, what percentage of these displaced persons were Croat?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: I will need to check from -- with my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection. That's outside of the scope of the report because the witness has testified and the report indicates that he conducted no analysis whatsoever as to the number of Serb displaced persons from the area. So to ask for a proportion of the total number of displaced by ethnicity is a question that the witness can't answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe Defence counsel has misinterpreted my question. I am actually not interested in the number of non-Serbs in relation to Serbs or any other ethnicity but, rather, within the Croat population itself. So I'm confining it to Croats. And the percentage of Croats out of the total number of Croats in the 1991 census that were displaced according to the 1994 database.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I don't understand the question, then, because if it's the number of Croats amounted -- as a percentage of the population of Croats, then that makes no sense. That's a hundred per cent. So maybe I'm -- either I'm not understanding the question and perhaps there could be a clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I will try to clarify it. I think it's obvious, but I'll try to clarify it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We have a number here of the number of displaced Croats -- well, first of all, we have a number of total persons displaced which is 76.226 persons displaced from the SBWS. Now, if we look over to the right, we see a figure that says 93 or -- 93.4 per cent of these displaced persons were Croats. Now that is for all three SAOs. What I'm interested in is just for the SBWS, what percentage of Croats were displaced based upon the groups that are within SAO SBWS.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this information, Your Honours, can be derived simply from looking at the appendices, and so it's available, but simply it's better that the witness performs this mathematical calculation for us on the record rather than leaving it to the lawyers to try to do it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I try to explain the questions and the answers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Before the war in the 1991 census, in the war-affected areas of Eastern Slavonia, there were 91.756 Croats according to the census. Of that number, 69.168 can be found in the database of the displaced persons, which is 75.4 per cent. These numbers are not directly stated in the report but they can be derived from the numbers that are provided in the appendices just by adding the respective amounts for the Beli Manastir, Osijek, Vukovar, and Vinkovci. There is yet another analysis that can be done here, which is to look at the number of displaced Croats from this area amongst the total number of people displaced from this area, which is 90.7 per cent. And here, Mr. Gosnell is perfectly right, this is not reflective of the true ethnic distribution. It is just the description of the data set. This is just the feature of the 1994 registration. Within this data set for the broader Eastern Slavonia region, over 90 per cent of those registered were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So -- and again, that's the -- the total number of displaced persons was 76.226, and out of those which were derived from the 1994 database, over 90 per cent were Croats? Just to make sure I have it right.

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And then the second percentage is looking at that number compared to the 1991 census and we get a figure of 75.4 per cent of the Croat -- of the pre-conflict Croat population in the SBWS was displaced.

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes. This is roughly the interpretation with the proviso that, of course, the population could have changed between the census and the date of displacement. So of course, people could have moved out for another reason. Children could have been born, people could have died. So there were a lot of other things that could have happened. But in general, this is the direction, with those provisos.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So that's a minimum estimate, more or less, the 75.4 per cent?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection, that's leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Right. Fair enough. Let's turn to figure 3, which is on page 9 of your report, 10 of the version on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Doctor, could you explain to us, what does this figure tell us about the pre-conflict ethnic composition of the SBWS as compared to the other SAOs?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to start by just reiterating that the colours -- colourings on this map refer not to the whole municipalities but to the war-affected settlements within these municipalities only. And with that proviso, it seems that the -- well, the Eastern Slavonia as compared to other areas, especially in Krajina and Western Slavonia, was in many places more dominated by Croats, even if the majority was a relative one, and by other non-Serbs. And by this, I predominantly mean Hungarians, which can be seen on the bottom chart denoted by the green colour. This is, by the way, an example of -- which shows the benefits of using the new municipal division as opposed to the old one because we can obtain a far more detailed picture of the ethnic composition of the area of the particular localities.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let us look at figure 8, which is on page 20 of the report, page 21 on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Doctor, could you tell us, what does this figure show us with regard to SAO SBWS as compared to the other SAOs?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: This figure generally displays the number of displaced persons from the war-affected settlements, again, plotted by old municipalities. And the top chart refers to the 1994 database. The bottom chart refers to the 1997 Eastern Slavonia registration and the requests for return. And especially -- one thing worth noting here is that the scales are different. The magnitude of the displacement shown in the top map is much higher than those -- of those in the bottom map, and clearly in the -- from the top map it seems that Eastern Slavonia region stands out in terms of the number of displacements per municipality. The highest -- the darkest brown colour refers to municipalities with over 10.000 displaced persons each and the numbers range up to 32 - nearly - .4 thousand. So clearly Eastern Slavonia stands out as the region most -- most displacements per municipality took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's now turn to figure 6 in your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is page 18 of the report. 19 of the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Doctor, you also conclude that the majority of the 182.995 displaced persons from the 1994 database were displaced in late 1991 from Krajina and the SBWS region. Did other sources available to you confirm this conclusion as far as when the most significant number of displacements occurred?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Both the literature that we reviewed as well as the independent estimates, such as those of the UNHCR, seems to be pointing out as to 1991 as the period of the most intense displacements from these areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what did your study find with regard to displacements in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: The general magnitude of displacements, as showed on the right panel of this figure, was much lower than of those that occurred in 1991, but still the figure shows that the displacements continued, although at a lower intensity, throughout the period under study. So they didn't finish in 1991. They continued throughout 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 40 of your report. And this is within appendix B. I believe it's B -- B1. And it's the municipality profile for Beli Manastir. First of all, if we could just look at the bottom of the page? Yes. And if we could turn to the next page. Perhaps I got the wrong page. I thought it was page 40 in e-court but it's the next -- it should be the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It was page 38. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Page 38. No, no. It will be the next page after that. And perhaps you can tell me what page that is so I can make sure that my future references are to the correct page. Yes, that's the one. Is that page 38?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is page 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. Then that is the one I want. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if we could look at the bottom of the page, could you tell us what's -- what's provided? What's listed down there?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page there is a list of war-affected settlements in the municipality of Beli Manastir as defined in the Croatian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So those are the -- the war-affected areas that you analysed?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. And could you tell us, just briefly, what information is provided in the first two tables?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: The top table, the top panel shows the ethnic composition of the population as enumerated in the 1991 population census by ethnicity, distinguishing the measured groups such as Croats, Serbs, Hungarians, Muslims, and a category of "others," which encompasses all defined and undefined categories including those who did not declare themselves. Further to the right there is an aggregate of the non-Serb population and a grand total for the municipality. The second panel shows a similar ethnic breakdown of the 1994 database of displaced persons. Again, the same ethnic groups and the aggregate and the total.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what about the two graphs, what do they show?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: They show the time patterns of displacements recorded in the 1994 data set, first for the period of 25th of June 1991 and the end of 1991, and then for the remaining period using a different reference scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You also found that 9.678 additional persons not found in the 1994 database were reported in the 1997 request for return Eastern Slavonia registration database as displaced within the geographical and temporal scope of your report. What did you conclude was the primary ethnicity of these persons, these 9.000-plus persons?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: For these persons about a third had their ethnicity stated as being Serbs and over 60 per cent had their ethnicity stated as unknown. And to find out who these people were, whilst we were in Zagreb on a mission back in 2003, we have matched this particular collection with a 1991 census in order to obtain a breakdown by ethnicity of -- for this collection. And basically for the whole collection of the 1997 Eastern Slavonia registration and requests for return, we found out that for those whom we have matched and had the ethnicity reported as unknown, about 90 per cent were Serbs in the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Doctor, do you have an opinion on why this subset of displaced persons for this 1997 database were primarily Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Well, I am not an expert on military aspects of population displacements, but from the analysis of the data it seems that basically mostly ethnic Croats were displaced into Croatian government-controlled areas, whereas ethnic Serbs were displaced to Serb-controlled areas of Croatia at the time, including Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And where were most of the 9.678 displaced persons from?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: From the -- from the numbers that I have analysed in this database, about a half came from Western Slavonia, a third from other places within Eastern Slavonia, and further 18 per cent from somewhere in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when was the peak for these displacements?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: The displacements from Western Slavonia peaked visibly in December 1991 with a magnitude within this particular data set of just about 1500 persons. The displacements from other areas in Eastern Slavonia peaked in December 1991 and January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry to interrupt. Could I have a page reference from where the witness is reading. I'd just like to know where the figures are from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's page 19 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe in your report you also mentioned that in this 1997 database there was 111.811 records. When did most of those displacements take place?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Most of those displacements took place in 1995 during and after the operations Flash and Storm and, as such, are outside of the scope of the current report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just briefly, because we are almost at our time for the break, looking at the Beli Manastir municipality profile that we have in front of us -- or, actually, now -- we've lost it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could we turn back to page 40 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Where do we find the data for the 1997 request for return and Eastern Slavonia registration database on this profile?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: The numbers can be seen in a small table at the middle of the page with a total of 132 persons and the graph of the time-line is shown underneath.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, would this be a good time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It would indeed. Dr. Bijak, this is the time for our first break. We will come back at 11.00. The Court Usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness, two short oral rulings. First one is about the Prosecution's motion to substitute Exhibit P1984.1981 with the revised translation, filed 31st of May. I take it the Defence has no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No objections from the Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The motion is hereby granted, and the Registrar shall take the necessary measures to implement the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: There is another one. For the replacement of Exhibit P1410 and 14 -- sorry, P1401 and P1402, filed 31st of May as well. Same position from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The motion is granted, and the Registry shall take the necessary measures to implement the decision. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Doctor, in your report you discuss how other sources, governments, international organisations, scientific literature, generally provide higher figures on the total number of displaced persons in Croatia during the 1991 through 1993 period than your figures from the 1994 database. Beyond the three provisos that you have already testified about, are there any other factors that would account for those discrepancies?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, as you may recall, we -- in this analysis we explicitly excluded the area of Dubrovnik and Konavle, so the very southern part of Croatia. Then we conducted additional quality checks and duplicate control on the data set. So -- and our temporal definition is also limited to the period from the 25th of June, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have on the screen table 5, which is page 26 of the expert report, page 27 on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Looking at the table, according to the data from the Croatian Ministry for Public Works, the number of Croat displaced persons, it appears from this table, reached a peak in 1991 or by the end of 1991 at 550.000 persons. But as we see by 1994, the number of displaced persons or persons reporting themselves as displaced was reduced to around 200.000. And that number appears to be quite close to the number you derived from the ODPRR database, approximately 183.000 displaced persons who recorded themselves as displaced in 1994. What does this -- what does this suggest to you, this variation or decrease over time?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Well, first of all the -- the closeness of our estimates and the ones reported in table 5 is not surprising given that the background data are the same data from the government Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees. As concerns the high variation in numbers, first of all, it seems that the statistics on displacements have become much more accurate later on. The 1991 figures obviously are rounded, possibly to the nearest 10.000 or even 50.000. So this is a very rough estimate of the number of displaced persons and might include many persons who have been displaced only for a short period of time, might include many duplicates. There is no way of actually verifying this first piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And were there ebbs and flows of the number of displaced persons over time?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Just by -- just by looking at the data from the 1994 database, there were clearly ebbs and flows. The highest numbers were observed in the second half of 1991, and then there was a pretty steady yet non-negligible stream of displacements from 1992 to 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I understand that. What I'm getting at is, we see the number of displaced going up or being -- starting up quite high but then over time it decreases. Could that be simply a matter of the number of people reporting themselves as displaced decreasing over time? Is that a possibility?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: That is a possibility. Another possibility is the returns, of course. Yet another possibility is that by the end of 1994, the registration already took place, so basically the Croatian authorities were in the possession of the database that is also the one that I am using for the report. So this was, by that time, the data the authorities had at their disposal were presumably much higher quality because they have been actually computerized and quality checked as opposed to, for example, the very high estimate for 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we see by this table, by the end of 1992, the figure is around 260.000 displaced persons. To what degree was that the accepted number amongst the various sources that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: There seems to be a consensus that by the end of 1992, the number of displaced persons in Croatia was about 260.000. So this is -- this is the number that appears in various publications as well as reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we also see the official statistics in this table for the number of refugees. Could you tell us where did these official statistics originate from?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: The data in this table come from the official registers of refugees or official statistics of the countries where the refugees actually were granted asylum. And here in this table there is a separation between Serbia and Montenegro, where the source is there the official statistics of Serbia and Montenegro, and other countries, where the source is the respective authorities of these countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I now want to look at some reports from the 1991 through 1993 period that provides some statistical information on displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: For the first one we are going to have to go into private session as it's a protected document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And may we have 65 ter 5917 on e-court. This is tab 38. And if we could turn to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see a chart showing the number of displaced persons in Croatia as of the 22nd of January, 1992, to be around 324.000. Now this figure appears consistent with the one we just -- the document we just looked at a moment ago; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: Yes. This -- this seems correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we see underneath the chart that the data is broken down by age and sex of the displaced persons. Could you tell us, just looking at the nature of these figures, are they estimates or are they a result of a count?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection. There is no foundation for that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, the foundation is his expertise as a demographer and a statistician. He can look at numbers and give us his views as whether they are just merely estimates.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is absolutely no foundation for the question. You can't tell that from looking at the document even if you are an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I tend to agree with that, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'll move on then, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now with regard to the data you derived from the 1994 ODPRR database, what percentage of the 183.000 displaced persons were female? And I'll direct your attention to page 16 of your report. We don't need to see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JAKUB BIJAK
utterances.text: So in both the 1994 collection as well as in the other, the 1997 Eastern Slavonia registration and request for return, the percentage of women was slightly higher than those for men, so it about was 52, 50 per cent women as opposed to 47, 48 per cent men, which is broadly in line with the 1991 census results which identified for the whole of Croatia about 51 and a half per cent of women overall, as opposed to 48 and a half per cent of men.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see in this document that women between the ages of 18 and 60 years old make up 22.4 per cent of the displaced population, while men of military age make up only 8.6 per cent of the displaced population. Could you tell us what factors may account for the lower number of men of military age or the age between 18 and 60?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. That's calling for speculation. There is no context and there is no basis to suggest that this expert has that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not asking the witness to speculate, but if he can provide an opinion based on his expertise, we would like him to provide it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Did the expert examine this, Mr. Olmsted?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, the expert witness has reviewed all the documents I'm showing him prior to his testimony, so he's had an opportunity at least to review them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You may answer, Mr. Bijak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect to this -- this question, what I found in this particular document, what I found striking was this gender imbalance in this age of 18 to 60 years which is clearly not there in the 1994 registration. And also the age structure, as shown here, is very much unlike what I found in the 1994 data collection. So there -- there are not -- basically limiting myself to my area of expertise, there are some discrepancies between the age and sex structures as reported in this document and to what I found in the 1994 data collection.
